caption:
How did a lake burp out a gas cloud you couldn't see?
In 1986 a quiet lake in Cameroon released a giant cloud of carbon dioxide. No wave, no fire, just gas 🫧 How Lake Nyos became a shaken soda bottle, and why people live there again, in 8-bit.

Sources (public domain, NASA and USGS):
- NASA Earth Observatory, Lake Nyos, Cameroon
- USGS Open-File Report 97-487
- USGS, Lake Nyos degassing

scenes.title: THE LAKE THAT BURPED
vo: This lake burped out a gas cloud you couldn't see.
Cameroon, nineteen eighty-six. No wave, no fire. So how does a lake burp?

scenes.title: LEVEL 1
vo: Fifty miles down, magma leaks carbon dioxide.
It seeps up into the lake's deepest water.

scenes.title: LEVEL 2
vo: Down there, the water's weight squeezes the gas in, like a soda cap.
But the deep layer never mixes with the top, so the gas keeps building.

scenes.title: LEVEL 3
vo: On August twenty-first, that deep water rose. The pressure dropped, and the gas burst out at once.
Nobody knows exactly what tipped it.

scenes.title: LEVEL 4
vo: Carbon dioxide is heavier than air, so it poured downhill,
at over sixty miles an hour. You couldn't outrun it.

scenes.title: THE ANSWER
vo: It pushed the air out of the valleys below, and the villages there had nothing left to breathe.

scenes.title: AFTERMATH
vo: Now a pipe lets the gas out slowly, a crack at a time.
The soil is so fertile that ten thousand people live there again.
